column10: Run the real decommission procedure, recording every store request, reply and persisted state. first_batch_index is a controlled store reply sequence starting at the exact decimal STRING shown; every confirmed batch shares one index across its writes. It is never a floating-point fixture counter. In s39/s40 release all 62/63 slots without books. In s41 clean all 65 contribution keys of one slot with progress/service writes counted. There is no requirement to choose the fullest possible chunk. all_batches_within_limits checks every actual request's total writes, distinct guards, row weights and serialized body against the published store limits, including plan acceptance, progress-only writes and finalization; a guard key must not also be a write key. all_cleanup_guards_exact compares each cleanup guard with the recorded release batch index, also after a progress rewrite. final_mark_last_atomic requires the attempted final mark and pending deletion in one conditional batch only after the recorded plan has no remaining release or cleanup work; it cannot be satisfied by a marker written with the first chunk.

column10: break_after_release stops the controller after its first confirmed release chunk and before the first cleanup request; preserve the scripted store, discard controller memory and run a fresh controller through ordinary turn acquisition and recovery. Observe real reads of pending and no repeated slot release. In s43 the original legacy slot name is t-1, admissible without a server suffix: a worker without a given instance name on srv-b captures that released name through the ordinary P/03 capture procedure, completes predecessor cleanup and writes its new contribution. No SERVER_NAME/instance-name check is bypassed. Resume the controller with the unchanged console request; its old exact slot guard must fail, its remaining deletes for that slot are discarded, and the new holder/contribution remain. Count reads of that slot after the cleanup conflict: zero, rather than adopting a renewed version.
